Before understanding "yardage," you need to know that a yard is a unit of measurement equal to 3 feet (or 36 inches). It's used widely in the United States and some other countries to measure distance or length.

Now, yardage simply means an amount, length, or distance measured in yards. The suffix "-age" signals that we're talking about a quantity or total of something — just like "mileage" means an amount of miles, and "footage" means an amount of feet.

So yardage answers the question: "How many yards?"
The Different Contexts Where "Yardage" Is Used

The word "yardage" appears in several distinct areas of life. Each one uses the word in a slightly different but related way.

1. Fabric and Sewing

This is one of the most common everyday uses of "yardage." When you go to a fabric store, cloth is sold by the yard. The total amount of fabric you buy or need for a project is called its yardage.

Think of it this way: if a dress requires 4 yards of cloth, a seamstress would say, "I need 4 yards of yardage" or simply "What's the yardage needed for this pattern?"

Yardage in this context tells you how much fabric is involved — whether you're buying it, measuring it, or estimating it for a project.

  • "Make sure you buy enough yardage before you start cutting."
  • "The yardage for this quilt is about 6 yards."

2. American Football

In American football, yardage is one of the most frequently used words in the sport. The entire game is built around gaining yards — teams try to move the ball forward, 10 yards at a time, to eventually score.

Here, yardage refers to the number of yards a team or player gains (or loses) during a game or a specific period of play.

There are several types of yardage talked about in football:

  • Rushing yardage — yards gained by running with the ball.
  • Passing yardage — yards gained by throwing the ball.
  • Total yardage — the combined yards gained overall.
  • Penalty yardage — yards lost because of rule violations.

Examples:

  • "The running back had 120 yards of rushing yardage in that game."
  • "Their total offensive yardage was over 400 yards."

Yardage here is essentially a performance statistic — it tells you how much ground was covered.

3. Golf

In golf, yardage tells you how far away the hole (or any target on the course) is, measured in yards.

Every golf hole has a yardage — it's the distance from where you tee off (start) to the hole itself. Golfers use yardage constantly to decide which club to use and how hard to swing.

  • "This hole has a yardage of 420 yards — it's a tough one."
  • "Check your yardage book to see how far the bunker is."

Golf courses also publish a total yardage — the combined distance of all 18 holes added together. A course might be described as playing at "6,800 yards."

Yardage in golf is essentially a precise distance measurement that shapes every decision a golfer makes on the course.

4. General Use (Distance or Length in Yards)

Outside of sports and fabric, "yardage" can simply mean any distance or measurement expressed in yards in a general sense.

  • "They measured the yardage of the field before laying the turf."
  • "What's the yardage from the house to the fence?"

This is the broadest and most literal use of the word — it's just asking or stating how many yards something is.

5. Livestock and Stockyards (Less Common)

This is a rarer, older meaning. A stockyard is a large enclosed area where cattle and other livestock are kept temporarily. In this context, yardage refers to the fee or charge paid for keeping animals in such a yard.

  • "The farmer paid a yardage fee to keep his cattle at the stockyard overnight."

Think of it like a parking fee, but for animals. This meaning is mostly used in agricultural and farming contexts and is not common in everyday conversation today.

Here is the big picture: yardage always involves yards as a unit, but what it's measuring depends on the situation:

  • In fabric/sewing, it's the amount of cloth.
  • In football, it's how far the ball has traveled or been moved.
  • In golf, it's how far a target or hole is.
  • In general use, it's simply any length or distance in yards.
  • In livestock contexts, it's a fee for using a yard (enclosure).

The word is always a quantity or measure — never an action, never a person, never a place. It answers the question "how many yards?" or "what is the yard-based measurement here?"

Think of yardage as the "yard version" of the word mileage. Just as mileage tells you how many miles a car has traveled or how far away something is in miles, yardage tells you the same thing — but in yards. Once you see that parallel, the word becomes very intuitive across all its uses.
